name: Watteau
lede: Watteau is a soft sky blue named for the French painter Antoine Watteau (1684-1721), and the pigment he is linked to in the books, Prussian blue, was brand new in his lifetime.

sections.title: A painter's name on a fabric color
sections.body: The color is listed in the Maerz and Paul dictionary of 1930 as first recorded in 1925, in plate 34 J 5, in the field of fashion and textiles [1]. That is two centuries after the painter's death, so the name belongs to the twentieth-century habit of naming dress colors after painters and styles. The swatch is a greyish light blue, about 10 CIEDE2000 units from [[sky-blue]] and in the same family as [[powder-blue]] [1]. No book gives the reason for the choice.

sections.title: Watteau and Prussian blue
sections.body: The reason to place Watteau in a color history is Prussian blue, discovered in Berlin in the early 1700s (1704 is the often-quoted date, though the Compendium calls 1704 to 1707 more reasonable) [2][3]. Ball says it was widely known across Europe by 1750 and was used by Gainsborough and Watteau [2]. The Pigment Compendium's survey cites at least one painting by Watteau among the earliest analyses showing it, together with a work by Adriaen van der Werff from before 1722 and two paintings by Canaletto of 1719-23 [3]. That puts Watteau among the earliest painters to use [[prussian-blue]] [3].

sections.title: Washed-out skies
sections.body: Ball points out that Prussian blue fades when mixed with a lot of white, as it commonly was in painted skies of the 1700s [4]. He names Watteau's *Récréation italienne* (about 1715-16), along with works by Gainsborough and Canaletto, as skies now pearly and washed out where they were once a deeper blue [4]. The swatch above, a pale greyed blue, is close to what such a sky now looks like, though the books do not claim it as Watteau's color [4].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: This blue appears over at least five per cent of the canvas in 166 of 23,781 museum paintings, within six units of CIEDE2000 [5]. Landscape painters dominate: Claude Lorrain, Philips Wouwerman and Renoir each have three, and Claude's rate is nearly fourteen times the archive average [5]. It is about 1.8 times as common in the 1900s as across the archive [5]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings; a color match is not a pigment test [5].

questions.q: Why are some eighteenth-century skies by Watteau and Gainsborough now pale?
choices: Prussian blue mixed with much white fades
The painters ran out of blue
questions.answer: Prussian blue mixed with much white fades

questions.q: True or false: Watteau used Prussian blue before it was widely known.

openers: Watteau painted with Prussian blue within a few years of its invention, and his skies have since faded to pearl.

issues: Hedged the 1704 date for Prussian blue
